subject_title: Ethics in Public Service and Knowledge of Law
topic_title: Indian Legal Framework: Court Hierarchy, Civil & Criminal Laws, Nirbhaya Act, and New Labour Codes
syllabus_mapping: Basic Knowledge of Laws in India: Constitution of India: Nature and salient features - Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy - Bifurcation of powers between centre and state - Powers of judiciary, executive and legislature. Civil and Criminal laws: hierarchy of civil and criminal courts in India - difference between substantial and procedural laws - order and decree - new developments in criminal laws, Nirbhaya Act. Labour Law: Concept of social welfare legislations in India, changing trends in employment and necessity for new labour laws.

content.text: Basic Knowledge of Laws in India: Jurisprudence, Court Hierarchy, Substantive vs. Procedural Law, Criminal Reforms, and Labour Codes

The Indian legal system belongs to the common law tradition, anchored by constitutional supremacy. A foundational understanding of law requires mastering the distinction between substantive and procedural codes, the structural hierarchy of civil and criminal courts, statutory instruments such as decrees and orders, modern overhauls in criminal jurisprudence (including the Nirbhaya Act and the Bharatiya Sanhitas), and the rationalization of social welfare labour legislations into four unified Labour Codes.

content.caption: Distinction Between Substantive Law and Procedural (Adjective) Law
rows: Definition & Nature
Creates, defines, and regulates the legal rights, obligations, duties, liabilities, and causes of action of individuals.
Prescribes the machinery, rules, conduct, and methods through which substantive rights and liabilities are enforced in courts.
Primary Objective
Determines 'What are the rights and liabilities' (e.g., What constitutes Murder, Breach of Contract, or Negligence).
Determines 'How those rights are enforced' (e.g., How arrest is made, how bail is granted, how evidence is admitted and trials conducted).
Statutory Enactments
Indian Penal Code, 1860 / Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; Indian Contract Act, 1872; Transfer of Property Act, 1882.
Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 / Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023; Code of Civil Procedure, 1908; Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023.
Retroactive Operation
Cannot be applied retrospectively in criminal law (Article 20(1) bars ex-post facto criminal statutes).
Procedural statutes are generally presumed to apply retrospectively to pending legal proceedings.

content.text: 2. Hierarchy of Civil and Criminal Courts in India

content.caption: Hierarchical Organization of the Indian Judicial System
rows: Apex Level
Supreme Court of India (Articles 124–147)
Supreme Court of India (Apex constitutional and criminal appellate court).
State Level
High Court of the State (Article 214–227)
High Court of the State (Can pass any sentence authorized by law, including Death Penalty).
District Apex Level
District Court (Presided by Principal District Judge)
Sessions Court (Sessions Judge / Additional Sessions Judge; can pass death sentence subject to High Court confirmation under Section 366 CrPC / Sec 415 BNSS).
Intermediate Subordinate Tier
Senior Civil Judge Court (Unlimited pecuniary jurisdiction in civil suits within district).
Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) / Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM); can pass imprisonment up to 7 years.
Base Judicial Tier
Junior Civil Judge / Munsiff Court (Limited pecuniary claims).
Judicial Magistrate of First Class (JMFC; can sentence up to 3 years and fine up to ₹10,000 / ₹50,000); Judicial Magistrate Second Class (up to 1 year).
Executive Magisterial Tier
Revenue Courts (Tahsildar, RDO, Collector for land disputes).
Executive Magistrates (District Magistrate, SDM, Executive Magistrate; handle preventive peace, Section 144 CrPC / 163 BNSS, unblocking public nuisances).

content.text: 3. Order vs. Decree vs. Judgment in the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC, 1908)

items: Judgment (Section 2(9) CPC): The reasoned statement pronounced by a Judge on the grounds of a decree or order. Contains a concise statement of the case, points for determination, the decision thereon, and the reasons for such decision.

Decree (Section 2(2) CPC): The formal expression of an adjudication which conclusively determines the substantive rights of the parties with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy in the suit. Can be Preliminary (further inquiries needed, e.g., partition suit) or Final. Every decree is appealable as a matter of right under Section 96 CPC.

Order (Section 2(14) CPC): The formal expression of any decision of a Civil Court which is not a decree. Usually deals with procedural matters, interlocutory applications, temporary injunctions, or appointment of court commissioners. An order is appealable only if specifically enumerated under Section 104 or Order 43 Rule 1 CPC.

content.text: 4. Developments in Criminal Law: Nirbhaya Act & The New Criminal Sanhitas

The Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013 was enacted on the recommendations of the Justice J.S. Verma Committee following the December 2012 Nirbhaya gang-rape case, establishing unprecedented protections for women:

items: Expanded Definition of Sexual Offenses: Broadened Section 375 IPC beyond penile penetration to include non-consensual penetrative acts; introduced minimum 20 years to life imprisonment for gang rape (Sec 376D), and capital punishment / death penalty for rape resulting in death or persistent vegetative state (Sec 376A).

New Codified Offenses against Women: Specifically criminalized Acid Attack and attempt (Sections 326A and 326B), Stalking (Section 354D), Voyeurism (Section 354C), and Disrobing of women (Section 354B).
Mandatory Medical Treatment: Mandated all public and private hospitals to provide immediate free first aid or medical treatment to rape and acid attack victims.

The Three New Criminal Laws (In Force from July 1, 2024): (1) Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS, 2023) replaced IPC 1860, replacing sedition with treason against sovereignty, adding organized crime, mob lynching, and community service; (2) Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS, 2023) replaced CrPC 1973, mandating forensic investigation for offenses punishable with 7+ years, timeline for charge sheets, and mandatory audio-video recording of search and seizures; (3) Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA, 2023) replaced Indian Evidence Act 1872, recognizing electronic and digital records as primary evidence.

content.text: 5. Labour Law Reforms: Consolidation into Four Labour Codes

To address shifting employment realities (contractualization, gig workers, platform work, automation), Parliament amalgamated 29 disparate, archaic colonial and post-independence central labour laws into Four Comprehensive Labour Codes recommended by the Second National Commission on Labour (Ravindra Varma Committee):

content.caption: The Four National Labour Codes: Consolidated Enactments and Core Protections
rows: Code on Wages, 2019
Payment of Wages Act 1936, Minimum Wages Act 1948, Payment of Bonus Act 1965, Equal Remuneration Act 1976.
Universalizes minimum wages and timely payment across all employees (organized and unorganized); introduces statutory National Floor Wage; prohibits gender discrimination in wages.
Industrial Relations Code, 2020
Trade Unions Act 1926, Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act 1946, Industrial Disputes Act 1947.

Raises the employee threshold for mandatory government retrenchment/closure permission from 100 to 300 workers; mandates 14 days prior notice before strikes; establishes sole negotiating trade union council.
Code on Social Security, 2020
EPF Act 1952, ESI Act 1948, Maternity Benefit Act 1961, Payment of Gratuity Act 1972, Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act 2008.

First statutory recognition of Gig and Platform Workers; mandates aggregators (Uber, Zomato, Swiggy) to contribute 1-2% of turnover to a National Social Security Fund; fixed-term employees made eligible for proportionate gratuity.
Occupational Safety, Health & Working Conditions (OSH) Code, 2020
Factories Act 1948, Mines Act 1952, Plantations Labour Act 1951, Contract Labour Act 1970, Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act 1979.
Permits women to work in all establishments during night shifts (7 PM to 6 AM) subject to their explicit consent and mandatory safety/transport arrangements; mandates annual free health check-ups.

content.text: Part A: Mains Analytical & Descriptive Questions

items:
Explain the structural hierarchy of Civil and Criminal Courts in a district. Distinguish between the powers of a Sessions Judge and a Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM). (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Detail the district judicial pyramid; Civil hierarchy (District Judge, Senior Civil Judge, Junior Civil Judge); Criminal hierarchy (Sessions Judge, CJM, JMFC, JMFC-II); explain the distinct sentencing capacities: Sessions Judge can pass any sentence authorized by law (including life imprisonment and death sentence, with death sentence subject to mandatory High Court confirmation under Section 366 CrPC / 415 BNSS); CJM can pass sentences up to 7 years imprisonment and fines; delineate separation of judicial magistrates from executive magistrates under Article 50.

Analyze the landmark changes introduced in criminal jurisprudence by the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013 (Nirbhaya Act). (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Contextualize Justice J.S. Verma Committee recommendations; detail legislative amendments: widening definition of rape under Sec 375 IPC, introducing non-bailable stringent punishments for gang-rape, death penalty for vegetative rape (376A); analyze newly codified offenses: voyeurism (354C), stalking (354D), disrobing (354B), and acid attacks (326A/B); examine victim-centric procedural safeguards: in-camera trials, recording victim statements by female police/magistrates, and mandatory free medical treatment.

Critically evaluate the necessity of replacing 29 fragmented central labour statutes with the Four Labour Codes. How does the Code on Social Security, 2020 safeguard the rights of Gig and Platform Workers? (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Outline historical fragmentation of Indian labour laws causing compliance burdens and informalization of labor (90% informal workforce); explain rationalization into 4 codes (Wages, Industrial Relations, Social Security, OSH); analyze the Code on Social Security 2020: statutory definition of Gig and Platform workers, creation of Social Security Fund funded by platform aggregators, toll-free helplines, portability of social security; balance ease of doing business against criticisms of relaxed hiring-firing norms under Industrial Relations Code.

content.text: Part B: Screening / Prelims Objective Questions

items:
Q1. Under the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC), 1908, a formal adjudication that conclusively determines the rights of the parties with regard to all or any matters in controversy in a suit is defined as a:
(a) Judgment
(b) Order
(c) Decree
(d) Plaint
Correct Answer: (c) Decree [Explanation: Section 2(2) of the CPC defines a Decree as the formal expression of an adjudication that conclusively determines the substantive rights of the parties.]

Q2. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), what is the maximum sentence of imprisonment that a Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) is legally competent to pass?
(a) Up to 3 years
(b) Up to 7 years
(c) Up to 10 years
(d) Life imprisonment
Correct Answer: (b) Up to 7 years [Explanation: Under Section 29(1) of the CrPC, the court of a Chief Judicial Magistrate may pass any sentence authorized by law except a sentence of death or imprisonment for life or imprisonment for a term exceeding seven years.]

Q3. Which committee's recommendations formed the bedrock of the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013 (Nirbhaya Act)?
(a) Justice Malimath Committee
(b) Justice J.S. Verma Committee
(c) Justice Sarkaria Commission
(d) Justice Mudgal Committee
Correct Answer: (b) Justice J.S. Verma Committee [Explanation: Following the December 2012 incident, the Justice J.S. Verma Committee submitted its report in January 2013, leading to the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013.]

Q4. Which of the Four Labour Codes first provided statutory recognition and social security funding mechanisms for 'Gig and Platform Workers' in India?
(a) Code on Wages, 2019
(b) Industrial Relations Code, 2020
(c) Code on Social Security, 2020
(d) Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020
Correct Answer: (c) Code on Social Security, 2020 [Explanation: The Code on Social Security, 2020 statutorily defined gig and platform workers and mandated social security schemes financed by aggregators.]

Q5. Under the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, what is the raised threshold of workers in an industrial establishment beyond which prior government permission is mandatory for retrenchment, layoff, or closure?
(a) 100 workers
(b) 200 workers
(c) 300 workers
(d) 500 workers
Correct Answer: (c) 300 workers [Explanation: The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 increased the threshold from 100 workers (under the 1947 Act) to 300 workers for seeking prior state permission before retrenching workers or closing down.]
